newsitem.title: COTE D'IVOIRE: Higher fuel cost may affect Ivorian produce prices.
newsitem.headline: Higher fuel cost may affect Ivorian produce prices.

text.p: Ivory Coast's 1996/97 cocoa and coffee marketing price structure, due to be announced from the middle of this month, may be adjusted to take into account recent gasoline and diesel price rises, government and industry sources said.
"Petrol price hikes could seriously hit producers if they are passed down the chain," a senior transport ministry official told Reuters.
"A price increase would probably be included in the bareme (marketing chain price guidelines), but it is hard to tell," a banking source said.
Fuel prices rose about five percent after government price-fixing ended on September 27.

Up-country buyers said they would not pass on the cost by shaving the recommended price they pay to producers, currently 315 CFA francs for cocoa and 695 CFA for coffee, but some wanted the new bareme to take account of the extra costs.
"It pushes up our costs and, yes, we want a change in the transport commission to reflect this," said a Gagno-based buyer.
A buyer's commission for collecting cocoa from farmers is about 33 CFA per tonne, and includes an allowance for transport.
Buyers say this should be increased to protect their net profits, but exporters say the price rise will have little effect on buyers' overall costs.

"I don't think it makes any difference to the bareme," said one San Pedro-based exporter. "Fuel is a small element of their (buyers') overall costs. The distances are not that great and I think they are more concerned about the level of import tax levied on spare parts and other costs," he added.

Economy and Finance Minister N'Goran Niamien said the move away from government fuel price fixing was aimed at lowering long-term gasoline prices by fostering competition in the industry, largely dominated by foreign oil majors.
Fuel station owners say the increases reflect higher oil prices on the world market.
